items.followUp: Why does an energy saver use less electricity than an incandescent lamp to produce the same amount of light?

rubric.why: This identifies the key comparison with an ordinary lamp.
rubric.description: States that it produces the same light using less electricity or power.
rubric.how: Award for both the same-light output and lower electricity or power use.

rubric.description: States that it is more efficient or wastes less energy as heat.
rubric.how: Award for identifying greater efficiency or reduced heat waste.

modelAnswer: An energy saver produces the same amount of light as an ordinary electric lamp while using less electrical power.
It is more efficient and wastes less energy as heat.

items.followUp: Define work and write its SI unit.

rubric.why: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done.
rubric.description: Defines power as work done per unit time.
rubric.how: Award for a correct rate-of-work definition.

rubric.why: The SI unit of power is the watt.
rubric.description: Gives the SI unit of power.
rubric.how: Award for watt (W), or joule per second.

modelAnswer: Power is the rate of doing work.
Its SI unit is the watt (W), equal to one joule per second (J/s).

items.followUp: Differentiate between concurrent forces acting in the same direction and in opposite directions.

rubric.why: Like parallel forces act along parallel lines in the same direction.
rubric.description: States the direction of like parallel forces.
rubric.how: Award for saying that like parallel forces act in the same direction.

rubric.why: Unlike parallel forces act along parallel lines in opposite directions.
rubric.description: States the direction of unlike parallel forces.
rubric.how: Award for saying that unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

modelAnswer: Like parallel forces act in the same direction.
Unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

items.followUp: Explain stable and neutral equilibrium, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: A stable body tends to return to its original position after a small displacement.
rubric.description: Explains the behavior of a body in stable equilibrium after displacement.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it returns to its original or equilibrium position.

rubric.why: A ball at the bottom of a bowl is a standard example of stable equilibrium.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of stable equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example such as a ball in a bowl.

rubric.why: An unstable body moves farther from its original position after a small displacement.
rubric.description: Explains the behavior of a body in unstable equilibrium after displacement.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it moves farther away or does not return.

rubric.why: A ball balanced at the top of a hill is a standard example of unstable equilibrium.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of unstable equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example such as a ball on top of a hill.

modelAnswer: In stable equilibrium, a body returns to its original position when it is slightly displaced; for example, a ball at the bottom of a bowl.
In unstable equilibrium, a body moves farther from its original position when it is slightly displaced; for example, a ball balanced at the top of a hill.

items.followUp: What does the prefix milli mean? Give one unit that uses it.

rubric.why: A prefix is placed before a unit to show a multiple or submultiple.
rubric.description: Defines prefixes in relation to units.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a prefix is written before a unit and indicates a multiple or submultiple.

rubric.why: Kilo, centi and milli are examples of prefixes.
rubric.description: Gives two valid examples of prefixes.
rubric.how: Award for any two correct prefixes.

modelAnswer: Prefixes are symbols or words written before units to show multiples or submultiples of those units.
Two examples are kilo (k) and milli (m).

items.followUp: What is the least count of a metre rule?

rubric.why: Least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can measure, or for vernier callipers the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division.
rubric.description: Defines the least count of vernier callipers.
rubric.how: Award for either the smallest measurable value or the correct scale-division difference.

rubric.why: The least count of standard vernier callipers is 0.01 cm.
rubric.description: Gives the least count in centimetres.

modelAnswer: The least count of vernier callipers is the smallest measurement they can measure; it is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division.
The least count of vernier callipers is 0.01 cm.

items.followUp: State Newton's Second Law of Motion and give one example.

rubric.why: Newton's Third Law states that action and reaction forces are equal and opposite.
rubric.description: States the equality and opposite directions of action and reaction forces.
rubric.how: Award for saying the two forces are equal and opposite.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates the paired forces acting on different bodies.
rubric.description: Gives one suitable example of Newton's Third Law.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example such as walking or gun recoil.

modelAnswer: When one body exerts a force on another body, the second body exerts an equal and opposite force on the first body.
For example, when a person pushes the ground backward with their foot, the ground pushes the person forward.

items.followUp: What is the second condition for equilibrium?

rubric.why: The first condition for equilibrium is that the resultant force on the body is zero.
rubric.description: States the first condition for equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the net/resultant force or vector sum of forces is zero.

modelAnswer: The first condition for equilibrium is that the resultant force acting on a body is zero.
